CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC → Increased HIF-1α expression → Upregulation of ENTPD2 → Enhanced conversion of extracellular ATP to AMP → Recruitment and activation of MDSCs → Suppression of CTLs and immune evasion → Resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors
Hypothesis: Targeting the HIF-1α/ENTPD2 axis to inhibit ENTPD2 expression in HCC will reduce MDSC-mediated immunosuppression, restore cytotoxic T cell activity, and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a complex tumor immune microenvironment that facilitates immune escape through multiple suppressive mechanisms. Among these, the hypoxic conditions within the tumor promote the upregulation of hypoxia‐inducible factor–1α (HIF‐1α), which in turn induces overexpression of ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 2 (ENTPD2). This enzyme converts extracellular ATP to AMP, creating a microenvironment that favors the recruitment and activation of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). The accumulation of MDSCs suppresses cytotoxic T lymphocyte activity and contributes to the observed resistance to immune checkpoint blockades. Here, we hypothesize that pharmacologic inhibition or genetic suppression of ENTPD2 in HCC will reduce MDSC infiltration, restore T cell effector function, and thereby enhance the therapeutic outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
